title: Hinduism: you are that
hookLine: a father dissolves salt in water to show his son the hidden essence: that is you (Chandogya Upanishad 6.13)
tomorrow: Hinduism: the act, not the fruit

lines: HOME FROM SCHOOL, A BIT PROUD.
THE THING THAT MAKES ALL KNOWN.
cards: A young man comes home after twelve years away at school. He's twenty-four, he's learned all the texts, and, the story says, he's a bit full of himself.
His father, a teacher named Uddalaka, asks him one question: did you learn the thing by which everything else becomes known? The son, Shvetaketu, has no idea what he means.
So his father starts teaching him again, from scratch, with ordinary things from the kitchen. A seed. Some honey.
A river. And a lump of salt.

teach.b: This is from the Chandogya Upanishad, one of the Hindu scriptures that explore the self and ultimate reality. Uddalaka tells his son: put this salt in a cup of water tonight, and bring it to me in the morning.
In the morning he says, bring me the salt. The son looks. It's gone.
Taste the water from the top, says his father.
From the bottom? Salty. The salt is everywhere in the water, though you can't see it anywhere.

teach.h: TAT TVAM ASI: YOU ARE THAT.
teach.b: That, says Uddalaka, is how it is with the finest essence of all things, what later Hindu teachers call Brahman, ultimate reality. Unseen, yet here, in everything. That is the real.
That is the self. And then: tat tvam asi. You are that, Shvetaketu.
Tat, that. Tvam, you. Asi, are.
The father says it again and again through this chapter, once after each picture. Hindu schools read these three words differently.
Advaita Vedanta, following the teacher Shankara, reads them as identity: your deepest self and Brahman are one and the same.
The school of Ramanuja reads a close unity with a difference, the self belonging to Brahman the way a body belongs to its soul.
The school of Madhva holds that the self and God are always distinct, and reads the line another way. All three are Hindu, and all three take the salt seriously: something invisible, in every drop.

how: Tat tvam asi is one of the great sayings of the Upanishads; Hindu students of Vedanta study it with a teacher, and the schools of Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva each explain it in their own way.

o: the priestly class that leads Hindu temple rituals
ultimate reality, unseen yet present in everything
the creator god who made the world, in Hindu stories

games.q: the salt lesson — tap the pairs.

s: all Hindus read tat tvam asi the same way
Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva's schools read it differently.
the father repeats the line many times in the chapter
again and again, each time after a different picture.
the son could see the salt in the morning
it had dissolved; he could only taste it, in every part of the water.

games.q: you're Shvetaketu. your father asks you to bring back the salt you put in water last night. what happens?
o: you can't find it, but every sip is salty.
games.why: the salt is gone from sight but present everywhere. that, says Uddalaka, is how the finest essence is in all things: tat tvam asi.

practice: If you have a glass of water and a pinch of salt, stir it in and take a slow sip; if not, just imagine it. You can't see the salt, yet every sip carries it.
Close your eyes and let the father's picture sit with you; you don't need to decide what it means.

wordCard.voice: Brahman. Ultimate reality, invisible yet present in everything, the way salt is in every drop of the water it's dissolved in. Today's word.
